opus-5.5.text:
I'd say our understanding is still pretty limited, honestly. We have a lot of empirical knowledge. We know what tends to work, what architectures, what training tricks, what scale of data gives you good results. But a real scientific understanding of why these models generalize the way they do is still mostly missing.

Classical learning theory tells you that if you have a model with far more parameters than data points, you should expect overfitting. Yet these massively overparameterized networks fit the training data perfectly and still do well on new examples. There's been interesting work trying to explain that: implicit regularization from stochastic gradient descent, double descent, the neural tangent kernel, flatness of minima, and so on. Each of these captures part of the story, but none of them gives a complete, predictive theory. We can't yet look at a dataset and an architecture and say with confidence how well the model will generalize before training it.

It's even more pronounced for generative models, which is the area I spend most of my time on. With something like a diffusion model, there's a real question of what it means to generalize versus memorize. If the model learned the training distribution perfectly, in some sense it would just reproduce the training data. So the fact that these models produce novel, high-quality samples means some inductive bias, from the architecture or the optimization, is shaping what they learn. Understanding that bias is, I think, one of the most important open problems.

So I'd characterize where we are as somewhat pre-scientific. We have a lot of phenomenology and some partial theories, but we're still waiting for something unifying. That's what makes it exciting to work on, though. There's a lot of room for new ideas.

r001.rationale: The response says current theories do not provide a complete predictive account, but does not clearly state that prediction fails at practically relevant scales, including for classification.

r002.rationale: It says the lack of understanding is “even more pronounced for generative models,” contrasting them with the broader discussion of generalization.

r003.rationale: It contrasts classical overfitting expectations with neural networks’ empirical success, but does not identify curse-of-dimensionality arguments or say they imply generative modeling should be infeasible.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting open questions in the field, honestly. We have these models with hundreds of millions or billions of parameters, far more parameters than training examples, and classical learning theory would tell you they should just memorize the data and fail miserably on anything new. And yet they don't. They generalize remarkably well. So there's clearly a gap between the theory we have and what we observe in practice.

I'd say our understanding is partial. We have pieces of the puzzle. There's good work on implicit regularization, the idea that stochastic gradient descent itself has a bias toward certain kinds of solutions, flatter minima, simpler functions, that happen to generalize. There's work on the role of over-parameterization, the double descent phenomenon, where adding more parameters past the interpolation threshold can actually improve test performance, which was very counterintuitive when people first saw it. And there's a lot of interesting work on the geometry of the loss landscape.

But if you ask me, do we have a theory that can tell you, before you train, how a given architecture will generalize on a given dataset, the answer is no. Most of the bounds we can prove are vacuous for the kinds of networks people actually use. So in practice, generalization is still largely an empirical science. People try things, they look at validation curves, they develop intuitions.

What I find encouraging is that the empirical phenomena are quite robust and reproducible, which means there is something real there to be explained. And I think the right approach is to take those empirical observations seriously and build theory that's grounded in them, rather than starting from classical assumptions that we already know don't hold in this regime. From my own perspective, a lot of my work has been on generative models, and there the question of generalization is even more subtle, because you can't easily measure it with a test accuracy number. You have to ask whether the model has actually learned the underlying distribution or just stitched together things it has seen. And I think that's going to be a very active area in the coming years.

r001.rationale: It says no theory can predict generalization for a given architecture and dataset before training, and that current bounds are vacuous for networks people use.

r002.rationale: It describes generalization for generative models as “even more subtle” than using test accuracy and asks whether they learned the underlying distribution.

r003.rationale: It contrasts classical memorization predictions with the observed generalization of large models, but does not identify curse-of-dimensionality arguments or connect them to the feasibility of generative modeling.

astra-6.text:
I think our understanding is still quite limited. We have these models that work remarkably well in practice, but explaining why they generalize so well is much harder. In many cases, they have enough capacity to fit the training data perfectly—even if you replace the labels with random labels. So the ability to fit the training set, by itself, doesn't explain why they make good predictions on new examples.

That suggests we need to look at more than just the size of the model. The structure of the data matters, the architecture matters, and the training algorithm matters. When there are many different solutions that fit the training data, which one does the optimization procedure find, and why is that solution useful on unseen data?

We've made progress on pieces of that question, but I don't think we have a complete theory. There is still a substantial gap between what we can demonstrate empirically and what we can explain mathematically, and that makes this a very exciting area of research.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no complete theory and a gap between empirical results and mathematical explanations, but does not state that existing theory fails to predict generalization at practically relevant scales, including classification.

r002.rationale: It does not compare understanding of generative models with classification models.

r003.rationale: It mentions model capacity and fitting random labels, but not curse-of-dimensionality arguments or their tension with generative-model success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think our understanding is still quite limited. We have a lot of empirical evidence that deep learning works remarkably well, but explaining why it generalizes so well is much harder. These models can have far more parameters than training examples, so some of the classical ways of thinking about generalization don’t give us very useful guarantees.

One thing that makes this interesting is that the capacity of the model alone cannot explain the outcome. You also have to consider the data and the way you train the model. There can be many solutions that fit the training set, and the optimization algorithm has some preference for which solution it finds. Understanding that interaction—between the architecture, the optimization procedure, and the structure in the data—is a big part of the challenge.

So I would say we have useful pieces of the picture, but we’re still far from a complete scientific explanation. And that matters when we want to use these systems in settings where the data might differ from what they saw during training.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific understanding is limited and classical approaches offer few useful guarantees, but it does not state that no existing theory predicts generalization at practical scales, even for classification.

r002.rationale: It does not compare how well generalization is understood for generative models versus classification models.

r003.rationale: It mentions empirical success and the limits of classical generalization thinking, but does not identify the specific tension between curse-of-dimensionality arguments and generative modeling's empirical success.
